source.title: An Evidence-Based Approach for Choosing Post-exercise Recovery Techniques to Reduce Markers of Muscle Damage, Soreness, Fatigue, and Inflammation: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis

paper.citation: Dupuy, O., Douzi, W., Theurot, D., Bosquet, L., & Dugué, B. (2018). An evidence-based approach for choosing post-exercise recovery techniques to reduce markers of muscle damage, soreness, fatigue, and inflammation: A systematic review with meta-analysis. Frontiers in Physiology, 9, 403. https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2018.00403
paper.abstract: How do commonly used post-exercise recovery techniques compare for delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), perceived fatigue, muscle-damage markers, and inflammatory markers? Participants: Healthy adults aged 18 to under 65 across 99 eligible studies; 1,188 participants contributed to the DOMS analysis and 266 to perceived fatigue. Sport and level: Competitive athletes, recreational athletes, and inactive adults across varied exercise models. Training or return-to-play context: Recovery after a single exercise session, not longitudinal training adaptation or return-to-play. Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Randomized, crossover, or repeated-measures studies in English or French; single recovery interventions with calculable effect sizes; combined modalities and duplicate data were excluded. Design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis following QUOROM and PRISMA reporting guidance. Exposure or intervention: Active recovery, stretching, massage, compression garments, electrostimulation, immersion, contrast water therapy, cryotherapy, and hyperbaric therapy. Comparator: Control or alternative recovery condition within included studies. Measurements and outcomes: DOMS, perceived fatigue, creatine kinase, C-reactive protein, and interleukin-6. Analysis: Hedges' g standardized mean differences with 95% confidence intervals; heterogeneity assessed with I² and moderator analyses by population, exercise, modality, temperature, immersion level, and measurement timing.
paper.tldr: This review informs selection of post-exercise recovery modalities when the immediate goals are reducing soreness, perceived fatigue, muscle-damage markers, or inflammation. Across modalities, recovery interventions reduced DOMS (SMD -0.78, 95% CI -0.94 to -0.61; I² 56.62%) and perceived fatigue (SMD -1.40, 95% CI -1.92 to -0.89; I² 33%). Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis following QUOROM and PRISMA reporting guidance. Exposure or intervention: Active recovery, stretching, massage, compression garments, electrostimulation, immersion, contrast water therapy, cryotherapy, and hyperbaric therapy. Comparator: Control or alternative recovery condition within included studies. Measurements and outcomes: DOMS, perceived fatigue, creatine kinase, C-reactive protein, and interleukin-6. Analysis: Hedges' g standardized mean differences with 95% confidence intervals; heterogeneity assessed with I² and moderator analyses by population, exercise, modality, temperature, immersion level, and measurement timing.
paper.findings: Across modalities, recovery interventions reduced DOMS (SMD -0.78, 95% CI -0.94 to -0.61; I² 56.62%) and perceived fatigue (SMD -1.40, 95% CI -1.92 to -0.89; I² 33%). Active recovery, massage, compression garments, immersion, contrast water therapy, and cryotherapy produced small-to-large reductions in DOMS (Hedges' g range -2.26 to -0.40), whereas the other reviewed methods did not. Massage, compression garments, and immersion produced large reductions in perceived fatigue (Hedges' g range -2.55 to -0.88); the other methods did not show significant effects for that outcome. Stretching and electrostimulation did not significantly improve DOMS or fatigue in the pooled analyses.
paper.limitations: Publication and English/French language restriction bias may have inflated effects. Substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity remained, and the interaction between the preceding training load and modality effectiveness could not be resolved. Blinding was generally infeasible, so placebo and expectancy effects could not be eliminated. Performance recovery was not evaluated, repeated use and combined modalities were excluded, and changes in soreness or biomarkers should not be assumed to equal restored performance. Additional transfer limitation (practitioner interpretation): the pooled populations and exercise models are heterogeneous, so a collegiate American football program should match modality choice to the session, next performance demand, athlete preference, and tolerance rather than treating the ranking as universal.
paper.practicalImplications: Massage, compression garments, and water immersion are reasonable options when short-term soreness or perceived fatigue is the target, but the expected benefit is outcome-specific. Recovery decisions should be individualized and should not substitute subjective recovery changes or biomarker changes for direct readiness or performance assessment.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Massage, compression garments, and water immersion are reasonable options when short-term soreness or perceived fatigue is the target, but the expected benefit is outcome-specific. Recovery decisions should be individualized and should not substitute subjective recovery changes or biomarker changes for direct readiness or performance assessment. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
